FOREWORD This Indian Standard (Third Revision) was xkqcd by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Natural and Synthclic Perfumery Mntcrials Sectional Committee had been approved by the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products Division Council. This Indian Standard was first published in 1961 and first revised in 1951, incorporating gas chromatographic method of analysis as an additional test method, since this method was yet to be standardized for introduction as rcfcrce method. Subscqucntly in the second revision, for determining the minimum purity as total alco1~ols (that is, citroncllol, nerd) GLC was made the main method. The wet method of andysis was also retained as an additional method, since it was felt that citroncllol is not ;t single compound but a mixture ofvarious compounds and resolution by GLC may be difficult at tirnes. In this third revision, the rcquircmcnts for citroncllol have been redrawn taking into account that citronellol produccd in the country commcrci:llly is avnilablc from any one of the natural essential oils like Citronella oil (Java type), Eucalyptus citriodom and Lemongrass oil. In fact. citroncllol produccd from any of these oils is not :I single compound but contains, to varying cstcnts, other compounds such as geraniol, citronella, dimcthyl octanol, iso-pulegol, and lhcir cstcrs along with traces ofncrol. Accordingly the rcquircmcnts ofodour, relative density, refracti\c index have been modified. New requirement of free citronellol contenl by GLC mcrhod ;mtl the total cstcr content ha\c been included. Citroncllol (CloHzoO) is one of the most import:rnt perfumery materials, widely used in various perfumes and is also used as an effcctivc sweetener in Iloral :md fancy formulations. Citronellol is found in a widevarietyofesscntial oils, namely, oils ofcitronella and geranium. Cilronellol csgcranium oil is lacvo -rotatory and is called `Rhodinol' in trade. However, citroncllol produced and available commercially is oplically inactive and is produced by lhe catalytic reduction (hpdrojicn:ltion) of citronella1 prcscnt in the oil of cirronclla (Java lypc) or oil of Eucalyptus citriodora or citral present in theoil ofLcmongrass. A sample of rhc material is dissolved in a suitable solvent, namely, cyclohcxmc and dicthyl cthcr and is injcctcd into the gas chromarograph, from where it is carried by the carrier gas from one end of the column to the other. During its movement, the constituents of the sample undergo distribution at diffcrcnt rates and ultimately get sepnratcd from one another. The scparrrlcd constituents cmcrge from the end of the column one after another and arc dclccted by suitable means whose rcsponsc is rclatcd to the amount ofa specific component Icaving the column. A-'1 AI'l'AI~A'I'US h-2.1 Any gas chromatograph capable of being opcrntcd under conditions suitable for resolving thc individual constituents into distinct peaks may bc used. Since normal peaks approximate a triangle, the area is measured by multiplying the peak height with the width of half-height.
